2. Social Distancing
The "6 feet" rule (approximately 2 meters) was not based on scientific data.

There was no convincing evidence that masks effectively protect the population from COVID-19.

Extended lockdowns caused immeasurable harm to the economy, physical and mental health of people, especially the youth - a group with the lowest risk of severe disease.
Closing schools was not justified by science. Children rarely spread the virus and rarely became severely ill, but they suffered historic losses in education, psychological damage, and deteriorating physical health (including a sharp rise in suicide attempts among girls aged 12-17).

5. Vaccines and Mandates
Vaccines did not stop the transmission of the virus (contrary to initial claims).
Mandates lacked sufficient scientific support, ignored natural immunity, caused harm, and seriously limited personal freedoms.
Promises that "get vaccinated – and protect others" turned out to be false.

6. Overall government interventions conclusion
The report directly states that many key measures (distancing, masks, prolonged lockdowns, school closures, and mandates) either lacked solid scientific basis or did more harm than good. Authorities and some of the scientific community actively suppressed alternative viewpoints (including the lab origin theory) and used censorship.

These findings are particularly strong because they are made not by bloggers, but by an official subcommittee of the US Congress after a two-year investigation with access to documents, testimonies, and internal communications. 📌 Bridges: How Assets Move Between Blockchains

Main Points
⏺ Bridges move tokens across chains by locking on one side and issuing an equivalent on the other
⏺ They unlock liquidity and DeFi flows, but bridges are among the most attacked surfaces in crypto
⏺ This post explains how bridges work — and where security usually breaks

1️⃣ Core Mechanic — assets get locked on Chain A, and an equivalent is minted/released on Chain B via messaging.
2️⃣ Bridge Designs — some are trusted, some are trust-minimized, but implementation details matter everywhere.
3️⃣ Risk Hotspots — smart contract bugs, compromised relayers/validators, broken message verification.
4️⃣ User Impact — many of crypto’s biggest losses happen on bridges: one failure can wipe out liquidity.
5️⃣ Risk Control — stick to battle-tested bridges, look for audits/history, split transfers, avoid fresh bridges with no track record.

Final Thoughts

Bridges create freedom of movement — but they’re a thin layer of trust. If the bridge breaks, access breaks.

🟠 Nine Major Firms Launch $15M Bitcoin Security Consortium

BlackRock, Coinbase, Strategy, Fidelity Digital Assets, Anchorage Digital, ARK Invest, Block, Blockstream, and Galaxy have formed the Bitcoin Security Consortium, pledging $15 million over three years to fund open-source developers and advance quantum-resistant security research for the Bitcoin network.

The initiative reflects growing institutional concern over quantum computing's long-term risk to Bitcoin's cryptographic foundations, with participants spanning Wall Street asset managers, crypto exchanges, and infrastructure providers.

The Middle East Teetered On the Brink of an Expanded War 🌍

The Middle East teetered on the brink of an expanded war on Thursday, after Iran and the United States reignited their hostilities and conflicts on other fronts threatened to draw in more countries.

For the first time since the conflict began in February, the authorities in Egypt said Thursday that the country had come under attack, stating that an explosion at one of its ports the previous day had been caused by an unidentified drone. 

Earlier, Saudi Arabia also acknowledged direct involvement in the war for the first time, after conducting joint strikes with U.S. forces on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq on Wednesday.

As the scope of the fighting widened, U.S. Central Command said Thursday morning that it had completed another “heavy wave” of strikes on Iranian targets, including military command centers and missile and drone facilities. 

The Jordanian military later said it had shot down five missiles launched from Iran. Iran has not publicly claimed responsibility for that attack.

Central Command said its latest strikes were a response to Iran’s launching ballistic missiles at American forces in the Middle East on Wednesday, when the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said it had targeted U.S. military sites in Jordan.

The fighting this week ended a dayslong pause in direct attacks between the United States and Iran and ensnared an expanding list of U.S. allies. 

Since the U.S.-Iranian cease-fire collapsed earlier this month, there have been repeated attacks on several countries in the region, including Saudi Arabia, but Wednesday’s drone attack on the port of Damietta was the first reported to have hit Egypt.

The attack ignited a fire on two ships, including a U.S.-owned gas storage tanker, and threatened to draw Egypt into the conflict. On Thursday, the authorities there said they were conducting a full investigation and vowed to take “necessary measures to protect Egypt’s interests and national security.”

At a news conference at the Oval Office on Wednesday, President Trump implied that Iran was responsible for the attack in Egypt, without offering details, and said, 
“We’re going to be hitting them very hard.” 
Iran has not claimed responsibility for that attack.

Even as the fighting between the United States and Iran expanded beyond the jostle to control the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the world’s energy supplies, ships attempting to pass through it were still facing significant risks.

The Revolutionary Guards said early Thursday that a fire had broken out on a tanker attempting to transit the strait using an unauthorized passage. Its statement, carried in Iranian state media, did not specify whether the fire had been caused by an attack.
